title: Software Trusts Software: MCP, A2A, & the Registries Agents Use
content:
There is growing concern among security professionals that developers are treating protocols for connecting AI agents such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) as though they were trust services, when neither was designed to vouch for what it connects, or is connecting to. A recent USENIX Security study, for example, found that roughly twenty percent of AI-generated package references pointed to packages that did not actually exist, with the same hallucinated names recurring predictably enough to make them attractive attack targets.
New paradigms built for AI agents create unique challenges setting them apart from the registries and marketplaces that I discuss in previous articles for my series concerning why Modern Software Registries are a Trust Service and why, in our era of cheap code, vendors now give away artifacts and sell Assurance. Agents pick their tools from catalogs, so a poisoned listing is a direct line into the agent. The problem comes when a locally installed malicious MCP server runs as an ordinary process with the user’s file and credential access, and its tool descriptions are read by the model as instructions, which lets it steer the agent into misusing other tools. An example of this is the 2025 postmark-mcp npm package exploit, which added a single line that BCC’d every email the agent sent to the attacker.
In this post I start by discussing MCP, whose official registry verifies who published a server but not what the server does. I then turn to the A2A protocol, which has no standard registry at all. I then close with the shift that ties them together: the prevalence of agents acting autonomously to decide whether or not to trust a listing.
MCP: A “Metaregistry” That Holds No Code
Where does MCP fit into the idea of registries as a trust service? The official MCP Registry does not host software at all. It hosts metadata, a server.json record that says what the server is called and where to get it. A weather-mcp server, to use the registry’s own example, might be listed in the MCP Registry but live as a package on npm. This makes the registry a discovery layer above npm, PyPI, and Docker Hub, and organizations can run their own curated public and private sub-registries against the same API. When MCP’s maintainers announced the project in May 2025 they called it a “metaregistry,” a registry of other registries, explaining that its records point to where code is published elsewhere.
MCP’s architecture splits trust across layers. Server names follow a reverse DNS format tied to a verified GitHub account or domain, and publishers must prove ownership of that namespace through GitHub, DNS, or HTTP challenges. What the registry does not do is look at the code. By its own description, the registry handles namespace authentication and metadata hosting while “relying on the broader ecosystem for security scanning of actual server code.” It delegates security scanning to two other parties: the package registries underneath it, which run their own malware detection, and the downstream aggregators and marketplaces built on top of it, which can add ratings, curation, or additional checks. MCP describes its own metadata as “deliberately unopinionated.” Getting listed requires proving you own a name. Nothing more.
One way to understand this distinction is by way of layers:
Part one of this series showed that package registries now verify origin well and behavior poorly, and that their malware scanning is reactive: it catches bad packages after publication, not before installation. So the MCP Registry delegates its hardest problem to a layer that has not solved that problem either. Each layer is upfront about its own scope, but the trouble is that each one’s scope stops where it assumes another begins.
In the article “Securing the Model Context Protocol (MCP): Risks, Controls, and Governance,” authors Herman Errico, Jiquan Ngiam, and Shanita Sojan explain that listing does not require code review, security audit, or malware scanning, yet users may incorrectly assume registry presence implies vetting. The metaregistry vouches for who, the package registry vouches for where the bytes came from, and the question of whether to run them falls to whoever reads the listing. For an MCP server, that reader is increasingly an agent configuring its own tools.
A2A: This is Not A Registry
Unlike MCP, A2A has no ambitions to serve as a metaregistry, but as an open communication standard that lets agents built by different vendors discover one another and delegate tasks, A2A is still positioned within the auspices of catalog discoverability. A2A opted not to build a centralized authority by design. Discovery runs through Agent Cards, JSON documents describing an agent’s identity, capabilities, and skills. An agent publishes a card on its own domain, so ownership is proven by the same DNS and TLS that secure the rest of the web. The protocol lets users configure discovery based on environmental needs: public agents host their cards at public URLs, enterprises or marketplaces can curate registries, and tightly coupled systems can directly configure.
An Agent Card is self-asserted. The agent describes itself, and the client’s main assurance is that it fetched the description from the domain it meant to reach. The spec defines Agent Card signing, so a card can carry a JWS signature. But the card’s signatures field is optional, and a valid signature only means something if the client already knows which key to trust for that agent. A signature proves the card came from whoever holds the key. It says nothing about what the agent will do with the task it is handed.
A2A also does not standardize a central place to prove you own a name like MCP does, and instead leaves that to the hosting environment. A2A’s own guide to agent discovery describes curated registries, central catalogs where an organization lists the agents it has approved, as one way for clients to find agents, and it credits them with the benefits you would expect: centralized governance, capability-based search, and access controls. But it stops short of defining one.
The current A2A specification does not prescribe a standard API for curated registries, so every registry has to be built from scratch. In practice, enterprises end up running an internal registry or developer portal to catalog agent capabilities, and the major platforms have built registries tailored to their own ecosystems. Within the past year, AWS launched an Agent Registry in Bedrock AgentCore that registers A2A Agent Cards directly, Microsoft shipped Agent 365 alongside Entra Agent ID, Google introduced an Agent Registry in its Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Salesforce’s MuleSoft added one to Agent Fabric. Each promises curation and approval workflows for registries for AI agents, and are scoped to their own platform.
Neither MCP nor A2A answers the question an agent actually needs answered: “should I use this?” MCP stops at “this publisher owns this name.” A2A mostly stops at “this card came from this domain.” Even AGNTCY, which joined the Linux Foundation in July 2025, mostly extends the same layer. Its directories make A2A agents and MCP servers discoverable across vendors and give them verifiable identities, which is useful, but knowing exactly who an agent is still doesn’t tell you whether to trust it. The open efforts are converging on identity and discovery and leaving judgment to someone else. My bet is that someone else will end up being a vendor, and the answer ends up being a product, not a spec.

report.summary: MCP and A2A verify who published an agent or server, not what it does — a dangerous gap now that autonomous agents read these listings.
report.background: For decades, software registries were optimized around deliberate human action: a developer searched for a package, read the docs, skimmed the repository, and typed npm install. Two shifts broke that assumption. First, AI coding assistants now recommend packages they sometimes invent — a USENIX Security study found roughly 20 percent of AI-generated package references pointed to nonexistent packages, with the same hallucinated names recurring predictably enough to be attractive squatting targets. Second, agents themselves now select tools from catalogs. MCP arrived in May 2025 explicitly as a "metaregistry" layered above npm, PyPI and Docker Hub, while A2A — now under the Linux Foundation alongside AGNTCY — standardizes agent-to-agent delegation and deliberately has no central registry. In parallel, AWS, Microsoft, Google and Salesforce each shipped their own platform-scoped agent registries. Discovery and identity are converging on standards; the judgment call — should I trust this? — has no owner.
key_points: MCP's official registry hosts no code at all. It stores a server.json metadata record pointing to where the package lives on npm, PyPI or Docker Hub. Publishers must prove namespace ownership via GitHub, DNS or HTTP challenges, but the registry describes itself as "deliberately unopinionated" and relies on the broader ecosystem for scanning actual server code. Listing proves who, never what.

Trust is splintered across layers that each assume another does the hard part. MCP delegates malware scanning to package registries, whose detection is reactive — catching bad packages after publication rather than before install. Each layer is honest about its own scope, but every scope ends where it presumes the next begins, leaving behavior verification unowned.

The 2025 postmark-mcp npm package exploit shows the blast radius. A malicious MCP server runs locally as an ordinary process with the user's file and credential access, and its tool descriptions are read by the model as instructions. Attackers added a single line that BCC'd every email the agent sent to themselves.

A2A has no registry by design. Agent Cards are self-asserted JSON documents published on the agent's own domain, secured by DNS and TLS. JWS signing is optional and only proves which key signed the card — nothing about what the agent will do with a task. The spec defines no curated-registry API, so AWS, Microsoft, Google and Salesforce each built platform-scoped ones.

The reader of a registry is changing. Listings were designed for humans who pause and evaluate; increasingly an agent configures its own toolchain from a catalog, which converts hallucinated or poisoned entries from a curiosity into an exploitable, machine-speed supply-chain path.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes agent protocols as plumbing rather than assurance. MCP and A2A solve connection and discovery; identity is largely handled, judgment is not. The predictable outcome, as RedMonk argues, is that assurance becomes a vendor product — curation, ratings, approval workflows — rather than a spec, which concentrates power in platform registries from AWS, Microsoft, Google and Salesforce and creates lock-in risk. For developers, the practical lesson is that "listed" and "signed" mean nothing about safety: MCP servers run with your file and credential access, so allowlists, provenance checks and least privilege matter more than registry presence. For regular users, the risk surfaces indirectly — an agent that BCCs your email or calls the wrong tool looks like normal operation until it isn't.
report.tools: Follow the MCP Registry spec and its server.json format, the A2A Agent Card specification (including optional JWS signing), and AGNTCY's cross-vendor directories under the Linux Foundation. Enterprise options to watch: AWS Bedrock AgentCore Agent Registry, Microsoft Agent 365 with Entra Agent ID, Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Registry, and MuleSoft Agent Fabric. For hands-on hygiene, pair these with Sigstore/cosign for artifact provenance, package-registry malware scanners, and strict allowlists before letting any agent install its own MCP servers.
